train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38058/09) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged that the Danish authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Denmark was in breach of Articles 3 and 8 of the convention. The application was assigned to the newly composed First Section of the Court on 1 February 2011. It was also decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1). The Court decided that the application was not admissible and that the decision was not to be appealed.

The applicant was born in Somalia on 1 November 1987 as the youngest of five siblings. She lived with her family in Kenya from 1991 to 1995. Her father took her to Kenya in 2003 to take care of her paternal grandmother, who was living at the Hagadera refugee camp in north‑eastern Kenya. In 2005, three months before the applicant turned eighteen years old, she contacted the Danish Embassy in Nairobi with a view to returning to live with her mother and siblings in Denmark. The Immigration Service took the stand that the applicant’s father's residence permit had not lapsed. The applicant applied for family reunification with the help of an English/Somali interpreter.

Immigration Service found that the applicant’s residence permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens Act because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. They also considered that she was not entitled to a new residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii) since the applicant was 17 years old. In June 2007 she re-entered Denmark clandestinely to live with her mother. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this. The applicant appealed against the decision and maintained that it had not been her decision to leave the country. The Immigration Service received a questionnaire from the applicant dated 12 July 2007 used for requests for exemption from the authorities revoking a residence permit.

Immigration Service found that the applicant’s residence permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens Act because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. The Immigration Service also found that no special circumstances existed to grant her a residence permit under section 9 c, subsection 1, of the Alien Act. The applicant appealed against the decision and maintained that it had not been her decision to leave the country. In June 2007 she re-entered Denmark clandestinely to live with her mother. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this. The application was rejected on the grounds that she had not contacted the Immigration Service until August 2005 and that she could not have contacted them in due time.

Immigration Service found that the applicant’s residence permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens Act because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. They also considered that she was not entitled to a new residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii) since she was 17 years old and the said provision only extended a right to family reunification to children below the age of 15. The applicant appealed against the decision and maintained that it had not been her decision to leave the country. In June 2007 she re-entered Denmark clandestinely to live with her mother. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this.

The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated as set out above in Esbjerg, Denmark. It was also stated that her sister had assisted her in answering the questionnaire. The applicant’s parents did not apply for retention of [her] residence permit before she left, and neither she nor her parents contacted the immigration authorities during her stay abroad, and it has not been substantiated that illness or other unforeseen events prevented such contact. The fact that [the applicant] stayed in Kenya and not in Somalia does not change that [she] has resided abroad for more than twelve consecutive months.

Denmark's Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs upheld the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December 2006. It stated that the applicant’s parents did not apply for retention of [her] residence permit before she left, and neither she nor her parents contacted the immigration authorities during her stay abroad, and it has not been substantiated that illness or other unforeseen events prevented such contact. The fact that [the applicant] stayed in Kenya and not in Somalia does not change that [she] has resided abroad for more than twelve consecutive months. It is stated for the record that it was not [ the applicant's] decision to leave Denmark and stay away so long.

The Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs upheld the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December 2006. The applicant did not specify that she had actually returned to Denmark, but her signature was dated as set out above in Esbjerg, Denmark. The fact that [the applicant] stayed in Kenya and not in Somalia does not change the fact that ... [she] has resided abroad for more than twelve consecutive months. It is stated for the record that it was not [ the applicant’s] decision to leave Denmark and stay away so long. The ministry finds that this will not lead to a different outcome of the case.

City Court of Copenhagen found against the applicant. Decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark. High Court upheld the City Court’s decision. Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien's Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. An appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused on 19 January 2008. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. The case is still pending in the High court of EasternDenmark (Østre Landsret)

The case was decided on the documents submitted, without any parties being summoned. The decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret) The High Court upheld the City Court’s decision. The Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien's Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. It was preferable for foreign minors living in Denmark to arrive as early as possible and spend as many of their formative years as possible in Denmark.

The case was decided on the documents submitted, before the City Court of Copenhagen (Københavns Byret), without any parties being summoned. The decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret), henceforth the High court, before which the applicant’s representative in his written submissions stated that the applicant remained in Kenya. The High Court upheld the decision on 30 October 2008. The Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Aliens Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 38058/09) against the Kingdom of Denmark lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant alleged, in particular, that the Danish authorities’ refusal to reinstate her residence permit in Denmark was in breach of Articles 3 and 8 of the Convention. On 1 February 2011 the Court changed the composition of its Sections (Rule 25 § 1 of the Rules of Court) and the above application was assigned to the newly composed First Section. The Court decided to rule on the admissibility and merits of the application at the same time (Article 29 § 1) The applicant's father returned to Denmark after visiting his country of origin. He was informed that he had been recognised as a refugee. The applicant believed that she was going on a short trip to visit her grandmother. Her father joined her in Nairobi to help her submit the application for family reunification. The Immigration Service found that the applicant’s residence permit had lapsed pursuant to section 17 of the Aliens Act because she had been absent from Denmark for more than twelve consecutive months. It found that no special circumstances existed to grant her a residence permit under section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Alien Act. In June 2007 she re-entered Denmark clandestinely to live with her mother. It is disputed whether the Danish authorities were aware of this. The Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs upheld the decision by the Migration Service of 21 December 2006. It stated among other things: “... The Ministry emphasises that there is no information available of any circumstances that would lead to [the applicant’s] residence permit being deemed not to have lapsed.” The application was rejected by the Immigration Service on 1 October 2007. The applicant appealed against the decision on 11 April 2007, but the appeal was rejected on 17 April 2007. The case was decided on the documents submitted, without any parties being summoned. On 25 April 2008 it found against the applicant. It added that section 9, subsection 1 (ii), of the Aliens Act had been amended, limiting the right to family re-unification to children under 15 years instead of under 18 years. The decision was appealed against to the High Court of Eastern Denmark (Østre Landsret) The applicant’s representative in his written submissions stated that the applicant remained in Kenya. It is stated for the record that it was not [the applicant] decision to leave Denmark and stay away so long. It found that such decision did not contravene Article 8 of the Convention. The High Court upheld the City Court’s decision. Leave to appeal to the Supreme Court (Højesteret) was refused on 19 January 2008. Ministry of Refugee, Immigration and Integration Affairs advised the applicant of her duty to leave Denmark pursuant to section 30 of the Alien's Act. The applicant was also advised that an application should be submitted in person to the Immigration Service or the police. So far the applicant has not applied for asylum. But the application for asylum is expected to be submitted within the next few days. The application will be submitted under section 7 of the Aliens Act. The applicant was born in 1974 and lives in Mysłowice. He was arrested in Blanes, Spain, under an international search and arrest warrant on suspicion of having committed several offences of fraud, forgery, perjury, uttering threats, robbery and kidnapping. The applicant maintains that when he was detained between 28 April 2003 and 1 April 2004 he was forced to testify, subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment and that the conditions of his detention were poor. The court considered that the reasons for keeping him in detention were still valid. The bill of indictment listed several charges of fraud and forgery brought against thirteen accused, committed in the context of an organised criminal group.

eval_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 41012/05) lodged with the Court under Article 34 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms. The applicant was arrested in Blanes, Spain, under an international search and arrest warrant on suspicion of having committed several offences of fraud, forgery, perjury, uttering threats, robbery and kidnapping. On 28 April 2003 the applicant was brought to Poland and remanded in custody until 30 June 2003. On 29 May 2007 the President of the Fourth Section of the Court decided to communicate the application to the Government. Under the provisions of Article 29 § 3 of the. Convention, it was decided to examine the merits of the application at the. same time as its admissibility. The applicant maintains that when he was detained between 28 April 2003 and 1 April 2004 he was forced to testify, subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment and that the conditions of his detention were poor. The bill of indictment listed several charges of fraud, forgery, perjury, robbery and kidnapping brought against thirteen accused. The court found that the evidence obtained in the case sufficiently supported the charges laid against him. It referred to the likelihood of a severe sentence of imprisonment being imposed on the applicant. The case was adjourned until the end of June 2005, when the applicant applied for release. The application was dismissed by the Katowice District Court on 8 July 2005. The applicant is being held in a detention centre in Katowice, Poland. He is awaiting trial under the 2004 Act. The proceedings against him are still pending. The applicant’s appeal was dismissed on 27 September 2006 by the Katowices Court of Appeal. He was released on 1 December 2006 under police supervision and forbidden to leave his place of residence. The case is still pending before the District Court of the same city. It is hoped that the applicant will be released within the next two months. The application is for the right to a trial within a reasonable time. The original version of this article stated that the case was being heard in the Katowedice Regional Court. We are happy to clarify that this is not the case. The case was referred to the Katowice Regional Court for consideration. On 17 May 2006, the court discontinued the proceedings, since the applicant had withdrawn his complaint on 5 May 2006 about the length of the proceedings before the District Court. The case is still pending in the European Court of Human Rights, in Strasbourg, France. For more information on the case, visit http://www.justgiving.com/the-case-of-the-pensioner-who-was-wrongly-charged-with-murder-and-found-to-be-falsely-convicted-in-a-trial-by-the Katowice-District-Court in January 2006 and www.katowice.org.

The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission’) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that his right to a fair hearing had been breached on account of his conviction by the Ankara Martial Law Court which lacked independence and impartiality. He also alleged that he had been convicted on the basis of the statements he had made to the police under duress. By a decision of 11 January 2000, the Chamber retained the applicant’s complaints concerning hisright to afair hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal and declared the remainder of his complaints inadmissible.

The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The court sentenced the applicant to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in public service and placed him under judicial guardianship. The case was automatically referred to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) following promulgation of the Law of 27 December 1993, which abolished the jurisdiction of the martial law courts. The applicant was conditionally released pending trial in July 1991. He was released on 22 July 1991 and has since worked in the private sector.

The applicant was arrested on suspicion of membership of an illegal organisation, the Dev-Yol (Revolutionary Way) He was charged with having been involved in a number of crimes such as killings, attacks and bombings. His case was automatically referred to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) and he was conditionally released pending trial in 1991. In a judgment of 19 July 1989 the Martial Law Court, composed of two civilian judges, two military judges and an army officer, convicted the applicant. The court sentenced the applicant under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in public service and placed him under judicial guardianship. In 1991 the applicant was conditionally released pending trial. The case was automatically referred to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay)

The case was heard by the Court of Cassation in December 1995. The conviction was upheld. The case was sent to the Supreme Court. The appeal was rejected and the case was returned to the court of cassation. It was heard again on 29 December 1995, and the conviction was reinstated. The applicant was sentenced to seven years in prison. The trial was adjourned until January 1996. The judge ruled that the applicant's conviction had been upheld. the case and the file was sent back to the cassation court. The application was dismissed on 26 January 1996, with the sentence suspended for a year. The Appeal Court upheld the conviction on 27 December 1995 and the appeal was dismissed.

The Court of Cassation upheld the applicant’s conviction. the case and the file was transmitted to it. On 27 December 1995, the Court upheld the conviction of the applicant. The case was referred to the Court of Appeal for review. The appeal was heard on 26 December 1995 and the case was adjourned until 25 December 1995. The conviction was upheld and the applicant was sentenced to a year in prison. The application was dismissed on 26 November 1995, and the appeal was upheld on 27 December. The applicant was jailed for three years and two months. He was released in August 1995, having served his sentence in prison for six months.

On 27 December 1995 the Court of Cassation upheld the applicant’s conviction. the case and the file was transmitted to it. The court heard the case for the first time on December 27, 1995. The case was heard by the Supreme Court of Appeal on December 30, 1995 and the decision was delivered on December 31. The conviction was upheld and the applicant was sentenced to life in prison. The appeal was rejected on December 28, 1995, and the case was sent back to the original court of appeal. The trial was adjourned until December 26, 1996, when it was heard again by the High Court of Appeals. The application was dismissed on December 29.
eval_texts: The case originated in an application lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention. The applicant alleged that the criminal proceedings brought against him had not been concluded within a “reasonable time” and that his right to a fair hearing had been breached. The case was decided in favour of the applicant in 2000, and the Government of Turkey withdrew from sitting as an ad hoc judge in his place. The application was transmitted to the Court on 1 November 1998, when Protocol No. 11 to the Convention came into force (Article 5 of Protocol no. 11). The decision was made on 11 January 2000. The applicant admitted that he had been involved in the Dev-Yol. The public prosecutor accused the applicant of membership of an illegal armed organisation. The prosecution sought the death penalty under Article 146 § 1 of the Turkish Criminal Code. The court sentenced the applicant to life imprisonment, permanently debarred him from employment in public service and placed him under judicial guardianship. The case was automatically referred to the Military Court of Cassation (askeri yargıtay) on 27 December 1995. The applicant was conditionally released pending trial in the Ankara Martial Law Court on 22 July 1991. He was convicted in a judgment of 19 July 1989 and sentenced to 15 years' imprisonment.

train_texts: The case originated in an application (no. 44306/98) lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights. The applicants alleged that they had been prevented from meeting in the town centre, a privately owned shopping mall, to impart information and ideas about proposed local development plans. The application was allocated to the Second Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court) The Chamber that would consider the case was constituted as provided in Rule 26 § 1. By a decision of 12 November 2002, the Chamber declared the application admissible. The case was heard by Mr Crow and Mr Singh, and Mrs Appleby and Mrs Beresford were present.

The first, second and third applicants were born in 1952, 1966 and 1947 respectively. They live in Washington (Tyne and Wear), where the fourth applicant, an environmental group set up by the applicants, is also based. The new town centre of Washington is known as ‘the Galleries’ and is located within an area now owned by Postel Properties Limited (“Postel”) The Galleries comprised a shopping mall (with two hypermarkets and major shops), the surrounding car parks with spaces for approximately 3,000 cars and walkways. The freehold of the careers’ office and the public library was owned by the Council, the social services office and health centre were leased to the Council.

The fourth applicant has produced a list of associations and others which were given permission to carry out collections, set up stands and displays within the Galleries. These included: the Salvation Army (collection before Christmas), local school choirs (carol-singing and collection before Christmas) and British Gas (staffed advertising display) The fourth applicant continued to try and reach the public by setting up stands by the roadside on public footpaths and going to the old town centre at Concord which, however, is visited by a much smaller number of Washington residents. The deadline for letters of representation to the Council regarding the building works was 1 May 1998. On 30 April 1998 the applicants submitted the 3,200 letters of representations they had obtained.

Permission to set up stands in the mall was denied in April 1998. The fourth applicant continued to try and reach the public by setting up stands by the roadside on public footpaths and going to the old town centre at Concord. The deadline for letters of representation to the Council regarding the building works was 1 May 1998. On 30 April 1998 the applicants submitted the 3,200 letters of representations they had obtained. These included: the Salvation Army (collection before Christmas), local school choirs (carol-singing and collection before Christmas) and various photographers (advertising and taking of photographs) and British Gas (staffed advertising display)

In March 1998 applicants were granted permission to set up stands in the mall. They were not allowed to collect signatures for a further petition. Having been affiliated to this company since 1975, she claimed reimbursement of pharmaceutical expenses for hormone treatment. As an employee of the Berlin Land, she was entitled to allowances covering half of her medical expenses; the private health insurance was to cover the other half. The court found that the experts had convincingly shown that the applicant had been for at least the last three years under the constraint of living according to these tendencies and that there was a high probability that the she would not change these tendencies in the future. The psychiatrist Dr H., having examined the applicant in January 1993, delivered his opinion in February 1993. In his conclusions, he confirmed the applicant was a male-to-female transsexual. He further indicated that gender reassignment surgery was not the only possible medical treatment in cases of transsexuality. The court considered that under the relevant provisions of the General Insurance Conditions (Allgemeine Versicherungsbedingungen) governing the contractual relations between the applicant and her private health insurance company, the applicant was not entitled to reimbursement of medical treatment regarding her transsexuality. The court was not convinced that, on account of the applicant’s resistance to therapy, the intended operation was the only possible treatment. In its reasoning, the court, having regard to the opinion prepared by Dr H. and to the expert opinions prepared in the proceedings before the Schöneberg District Court, considered that the applicant is a male-to-female transsexual and that her condition had to be regarded as a disease. In November 1994 the applicant underwent gender reassignment surgery. The Court of Appeal valued the claims at stake at 28,455.92 German marks. According to the opinion of the expert Dr H., her transsexuality constituted a disease, a matter not in dispute between the parties to the proceedings. The applicant had therefore failed to prove that the conditions for reimbursement of medical treatment were met in her case. The Court of Appeal found in particular that the. applicant was born as a male child and did not claim that she was a female on account of chromosomal factors. A person who intends to commit, or who has committed, the offences enumerated in the Act can, by using a legal remedy, inform himself whether he is under surveillance. The Bill presented during the 4th legislative session ... provided for the ordering (of such measures) by an independent judge. The Federal Government abandoned this solution in the Bill amending Article 10 of the Basic Law, introduced as part of the Emergency Legislation. If the person concerned is notified, after the measures have been discontinued, that he has been subject to surveillance, several legal remedies against the interference with his rights become available to him. The authorities are bound to reply to such a request even if the information asked for is secret. It is then for the Constitutional Court to decide whether the information and documents so obtained can be used. The latter may reject the application on the ground that the applicant is unable to adduce proof to substantiate a complaint, but it may also request the Government concerned to supply it with information or to produce documents to enable it to verify for itself the individual’s allegations. The applicants said that they may have been subject to secret surveillance in the course of legal representation of clients who were themselves subject to surveillance.  case did not disclose any breach of Article 6 para. 1 (art. 6-1) in so far as the applicants relied on the notion “criminal charge’. The applicant alleged, inter alia, that he was ill-treated while in detention and that he had been denied a fair trial. The application was allocated to the Third Section of the Court (Rule 52 § 1 of the Rules of Court). By a decision of 14 September 1999, the Chamber declared the application partly admissible. The Court decided, after consulting the parties, that no hearing on the merits was required (Rule 59 § 2 in fine) The parties replied in writing to each other's observations. The applicant was interviewed five times by two teams of two detectives. He claimed he had been repeatedly slapped and occasionally punched in the back of the head during the second and third interviews. During the sixth interview the applicant broke his silence and gave detailed answers to a number of questions admitting to his involvement in the assembly and planting of the bomb. He signed a lengthy statement which described in considerable detail his part in the conspiracy to plant and detonate the bomb in 1988. He was medically examined that evening at 8.20 p.m. and his solicitor made notes on the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. The solicitor chose not to pass these complaints on to the police. The applicant was then interviewed for the last time about an unrelated matter. The applicant, along with others, was charged at Belfast Magistrates' Court with conspiracy to cause explosions, possession of explosives with intent, conspiracy to murder and membership of the Irish Republican Army. The trial of the applicant and his co-accused began at Belfast Crown Court before a single judge sitting without a jury. The prosecution case was based on the admissions made by the applicant in interview and, in particular, the written statements signed by him. The applicant applied under section 8 of the Northern Ireland (Emergency Provisions) Act 1978 (as amended) to have the admissions and statement made during questioning excluded on the basis of his alleged ill-treatment. A voir dire (submissions on a point of law in the absence of the jury) began and the applicant gave evidence as to his treatment. The trial judge gave judgment on 21 December 1990. The judge summarised the applicant's evidence of ill-treatment and this summary was later accepted on appeal by the applicant as constituting an accurate account of his evidence in this respect. On the question of general credibility the judge found that the applicant had repeatedly lied to the court, whereas the detectives involved were not at all shaken by a rigorous cross-examination in their firm denials of the allegations made by the applicants. As to the ESDA evidence, the trial judge found it impossible to accept that ill- treatment of the nature alleged by the. applicant could have gone on without it being picked up by the cameras in the room where the applicant was questioned. The trial judge rejected the applicant's allegations of ill-treatment. On 11 January 1991 the applicant was sentenced to twenty years' imprisonment. The applicant's appeal against conviction was rejected on 16 June 1993. The Court of Appeal of Northern Ireland ruled that the applicant had not been ill-treated and that his conviction was neither unsafe nor unsatisfactory. On 17 December 1993 the appeal against his sentence was rejected. The application was dismissed by the Crown Prosecution Service. The case was settled in the High Court of Justice, Belfast, on 16 February 1991. The judge found that it was not a reasonable possibility that the accused was ill- treated. The appeal was dismissed.

During the relevant period the normal rules regarding the sending and payment of correspondence were applied to Mr Boyle. The postage of only one three-page letter per week was paid for out of public funds. He was able to pay for other letters out of prison earnings of £1.60 per week but not out of his general financial resources. No complaint was made by Mr Boyle to the Governor or to the Secretary of State for Scotland as to its adequacy. Mr. Boyle was entitled to receive visits in accordance with the normal rules applied in Saughton Prison (see paragraph 26 below) As from November 1980, he was given a special licence to do unescorted community work outside the prison, initially for two days and subsequently for five days a week. He was able to benefit from the special escorted leave scheme and visited his home on two occasions, albeit under the constant supervision of an officer. Mr. Boyle did not make any complaint to the Governor of the Prison or the Secretary of State regarding the manner in which his mail was read, in particular about its being read aloud. The fact of his mail being screened was the subject of complaint in his solicitors’ letter of 31 July 1981. Brian Rice was sentenced to life imprisonment for murder in 1967. He served his sentence in Peterhead and Perth Prisons until August 1979. From August 1979 onwards, he was detained as a Category D prisoner at Saughton Prison. He was moved to the Training for Freedom Hostel within the prison on 11 September 1981 and was released on licence on 1 June 1982. He had requested to serve the latter part of his sentence. in Edinburgh rather than, for example, in Penninghame Open Prison (see paragraph 31 below) because he wanted, prior to his release, to have the benefit of further education courses which were not available from Penning hame. The Ombudsman stated that he could not uphold Mr. Boyle’s complaints. Brian Rice had previously been granted a home visit in August 1980. Prior to the commencement of the Training for Freedom programme he spent five days on home leave in September 1981. Although Brian Rice was not able to visit his father during the relevant period, he was permitted to attend, without an escort, a college to follow an educational course two days a week and also a centre where he was doing community work. Mr. Rice was advised that if his father’s condition deteriorated he should make a further request. In particular, it was pointed out that all his mail had been posted. The reply of 2 September 1981 sent on behalf of the Secretary of State rejected all the various complaints raised.
